$comment: Design tokens — the single source of truth for both client languages. Angular consumes the generated CSS custom properties; Flutter consumes the generated Dart. Edit this file, never the generated output.
$structure: Two layers. `color`, `space`, `radius`, `font`, `shadow` and `motion` are primitives — raw values with no opinion about where they are used. `theme.light` and `theme.dark` are the semantic layer: they name a job (surface, border, text-muted) and point at a primitive. Components must only ever use the semantic layer, because that is what makes dark mode a token swap rather than a rewrite. A component that reaches for --color-brand-500 directly is a component that will be unreadable in one theme.
$brand: Green #08911F and gold #D2CC06 with Poppins, taken from the live platform. This is myFiesta's existing identity — customers already recognise it, it is on the app store listings and the printed material, and a rebuild that arrives in different colours reads as a different company.

color.$neutral: Biased a few degrees toward the brand's green rather than a pure grey. A pure mid-grey next to a saturated green reads as unconsidered; the bias is small enough that nobody names it and large enough that the page feels like one palette.
color.$semantic: Danger is deliberately not the brand colour. The live platform sets --ion-color-danger to the same green as --ion-color-primary, so a destructive confirmation and a primary action are the same button — that is a bug worth not carrying over.

font.$family: Poppins, self-hosted as woff2 rather than linked from Google Fonts. A font request to a third party on every page load is a render-blocking dependency on somebody else's uptime, and in both launch markets it is also a privacy disclosure nobody consented to.

$shadow: Tinted with the brand's hue rather than pure black. A neutral-black shadow over a green-tinted surface reads as dirty; the tint is what makes a raised card look lit rather than smudged.

light.$field-border: Separate from border-strong because the requirement is different. A divider is decoration; the edge of an input is how somebody knows there is an input there, and WCAG 1.4.11 puts that at 3:1. Reusing the decorative border here measures 1.67:1 — visible to whoever designed it on a good monitor, and not to anyone else.
light.$primary: brand-600 rather than the brand 500 as the interactive fill. White on #08911f measures 4.13:1, which is under WCAG AA for the 14px semibold a button label actually is. The hue is unchanged — the step moves, which is what a brand colour is a ramp for.

theme.$dark: Not an inversion. The brand green at #08911f is too dark to read on a dark ground, so the primary steps up to the 300 and its text goes dark green — the accent keeps working in both themes rather than being quietly illegible in one.
